title: "College is a scam"
claim: College is a scam. Look at that guy who dropped out and became a millionaire, and I've got a master's degree and I'm stuck living with my parents.
fair: There's a real point here: the job market has changed, some majors have little demand, tuition and student loans can be heavy, and practical skills matter a lot.

analysis.text: The dropout millionaire is one story. It tells you nothing about the millions of people without degrees who are struggling.
We hear about the people who made it without a degree. Nobody makes a viral video about the ones who didn't. So the picture looks rosier than reality.
The claim boxes you in between "degree" and "real work." But there's a third option: a degree plus practical skills.

verdict: The frustration behind it is real and understandable, but the evidence is individual stories. A better question: which degree, combined with what, in which job market, at what cost?

title: "Things were better back in the day"
claim: Back in the day, people were nicer, neighbors looked out for each other, food tasted better, and kids had respect. This generation is ruined.
fair: Some things really have changed. In a lot of places, people know their neighbors less than they used to, and screen time has gone way up.

analysis.text: We remember the good parts of the past and forget the diseases that had no cure and the things most people couldn't access.
Bad things in the present grab our attention more, so the present feels worse than it really is.
"This generation is ruined" judges millions of people based on a handful of videos and moments.
Something existing in the past doesn't make it better. And nearly every generation has said the same thing about the one after it.

verdict: Nostalgia is a natural, even lovely feeling, but it isn't evidence. Compare one specific thing with actual numbers, not all of "back then" with all of "now."

title: "Everyone's buying it, so it must be good"
claim: This passive-income course has 50,000 students, and every comment is raving about it. It's definitely going to change my life.
fair: A big number of buyers can be a sign that something is useful. And other people's reviews are information worth having.

analysis.text: Lots of people buying something means the marketing worked. It doesn't necessarily mean the product is good.
The moment you see a huge number, you feel like you'll miss out if you don't buy. That's the herd talking.
The comments you see may be hand-picked, and the negative ones may have been deleted.

verdict: The numbers tell you the course is popular, not that it's right for you. Look for reviews somewhere other than the seller's page, and ask: what exactly will this teach me? Blind Spot Lab isn't financial advice.

title: "I tried it and got better"
claim: I had a cold, drank this ginger-turmeric shot for 3 days, and it went away completely. So it cures colds. Try it!
fair: Feeling better is real, and some warm drinks really can soothe a sore throat and ease symptoms.

analysis.text: Colds usually clear up on their own within days. Drinking the shot and then getting better doesn't mean the shot is what made you better.
One person's experience isn't the same as a trial with a group of people, where half get the drink and half don't.
Being "natural" doesn't guarantee something is safe or effective. Plenty of natural things can hurt you.

verdict: The shot might make you feel better, but this evidence isn't enough to say it "cures" anything. If your symptoms drag on, see a doctor. Blind Spot Lab isn't medical advice.
